newsitem.title: USA: Aetna Q1 up, helped by one-time gain.
newsitem.headline: Aetna Q1 up, helped by one-time gain.

text.p: Aetna Inc's first-quarter operating earnings were slightly better than Wall Street's expectations, but included a one-time gain that inflated the upside surprise, analysts said on Tuesday.
The results included a one-time gain related to the reduction of a severance and facilities reserve, they said.
Aetna earlier on Tuesday reported first-quarter operating earnings of $1.14 per share, compared to $1.07 a year ago.
The market expected earnings of about $1.05, according to First Call analysts' consensus estimates.
However, analysts said that the real operating earnings, including the reserve reduction, were about $1.07, only slightly higher than expectations.
Aetna shares surged 5-7/8 to 96-1/2 at 1412 EDT, on volume of 1.6 million shares.
Analysts said they were surprised by the sharp upswing, particularly in light of Aetna's giving lower guidance for enrollment in their Medicare product line.
"It's a quality of earnings issue," said an analyst. "Aetna's upside surprise was driven entirely by a one-time, non-recurring reversal of a reserve, which is a non-cash, non-operating reversal."
Analysts said they did not believe Aetna was deceptive in its earnings report.

"What they did in this quarter is that they believe that they are ahead of schedule in some of those SG&A (selling, general and administrative) savings projections, and therefore they drew down the reserve, on an after-tax basis, about $9 million," said Jim Lane, analyst at Dillon Read & Co.

Analysts said it was difficult to get a firm grasp of Aetna's true financial picture, because the dust has not yet settled from the company's 1996 $8.9 billion acquisition and merger with U.S. Healthcare.
"The problem is that it's hard for a company in transition, like they are, to get a real hard fix as to how things are going," said Ira Zuckerman, vice president of Nutmeg Securities.

"On the plus side, they indicated that their expense savings are coming through somewhat faster than they expected. On the negative side, (HMO) membership growth was muted, was a little below their plans," Zuckerman said.
Aetna said that commercial HMO and point of service enrollment rose by 10 percent and 13 percent respectively over the first quarter of 1996 on a pro-forma basis.
"It was a mixed bag, and I can't read a lot into the quarter," Zuckerman said.

"The big question is, future growth in terms of membership, the ability to raise prices in the face of rising costs. They seem to be making a big push in the Medicare business... (but) what's happening in Washington will affect that."
